1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5.strategy: The most testing and most analysed move: the bishop leans on the knight that guards e5, so Black has to watch that pawn, while White develops and prepares to castle. White plays for a lasting pawn centre and a long manoeuvring struggle in which Black has many ways to answer.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5.name: Ruy Lopez
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5.background: Named after Ruy López de Segura, a Spanish priest who analysed it in his book of 1561, although the Göttingen manuscript of about 1490 already contains it. It became widely popular only in the mid-nineteenth century, after Carl Jaenisch published a detailed article on 1.e4 e5 in 1847.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once: the d-pawn challenges e5, and after the pawn trade White's pieces get open lines. White gives up the central tension early, so Black can equalise with accurate play, but the game stays lively and avoids the heaviest theory.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4.name: Scotch Game
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4.background: Ercole del Rio was the first author to mention it, in 1750, and the name comes from a correspondence match between Edinburgh and London in 1824. It declined by 1900, and Garry Kasparov led its revival in the late twentieth century.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop with a target: from c4 it attacks f7, where only the king defends. Easy to play and rich in tactics, it lets White choose between a slow build-up and a quick central strike, but it puts no pressure on the knight that guards e5.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4.name: Italian Game
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4.background: Developed in the sixteenth century by players such as Pedro Damiano and Giulio Polerio, it features prominently in the game collections of Gioachino Greco from the 1620s. The name Italian Game was not common in English until the late twentieth century.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c4.strategy: A flank move that controls d5, so Black's pieces find less room in the centre. But it puts no pressure on e5 and spends a tempo on a pawn move, so Black develops freely and White has little to show for the unusual set-up.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c4.name: King's Pawn Game: Dresden Opening

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, but from g2 the bishop would see only its own knight on f3, and it could already come out more actively. Nothing presses on e5, so Black can take its time and set up the centre.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.g3.name: King's Knight Opening: Konstantinopolsky

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2.strategy: A modest developing move that prepares castling but leaves the bishop passive on e2, where it presses on nothing. Black can develop with a threat against the loose e4 pawn, and White has to spend a move defending it.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2.name: King's Pawn Game: Tayler Opening

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d3.strategy: Solid but timid: it guards e4 and frees the queen's bishop, but it closes the king's bishop's route to c4 and b5 and passes up any fight for the centre. Black develops at leisure and White gets a cramped, passive game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3.strategy: Prepares to build a broad pawn centre, but spends a tempo on a pawn instead of a piece, takes c3 from the queen's knight and leaves White behind in development. Black can strike back in the centre at once, so this is a sharp surprise weapon rather than a main line.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3.name: Ponziani Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3.background: One of the oldest known openings, discussed in print by 1497. Howard Staunton advocated it in his Chess-Player's Handbook of 1847, and for some decades it was often called Staunton's Opening; today it bears the name of Domenico Lorenzo Ponziani, who analysed it in 1769.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the second knight and guards e4, a solid and symmetrical choice that asks little of Black. It takes the c3 square from the pawn, so White gives up a broad pawn centre built with the c-pawn and usually gets a quiet, often drawish game.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3.name: Three Knights Opening

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn, but Black takes it with the bishop, which develops on the way. White's compensation does not make up for the pawn, so the gambit is unsound.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.b4.name: King's Pawn Game: Pachman Wing Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.b4.background: Presumably named after Luděk Pachman, the German-Czechoslovak player and author.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5.strategy: Gives up a knight for a pawn: Black takes it with the knight, and when d4 attacks that knight it simply steps back. White is a whole piece down for one pawn and has nothing to show for it.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5.name: Irish Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5.background: The earliest published game with it dates from 1899, played against Harry Nelson Pillsbury in a simultaneous exhibition in Chicago and reported by the Brooklyn Daily Eagle, which called the line the Chicago Gambit. The name Irish Gambit comes from a joke article in the Columbia Chess Chronicle in 1887.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6.strategy: The question to the bishop that defines the main line: Black finds out at once whether White means to give up the bishop for the knight. If White takes, Black gets the two bishops for doubled pawns; if White retreats, the bishop stays aimed at the knight that guards e5 but can be chased again with ...b5 whenever Black likes.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a threat to e4 and simply ignores the bishop: Black can take the pawn and White regains it, so nothing is lost. The line leads to solid, drawish positions, often an early queen trade in which Black has the bishop pair against a kingside pawn majority.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nge7.strategy: Defends the knight with the other knight, so after a capture on c6 Black recaptures with the knight and keeps the pawns intact. The cost is that the knight blocks the king's bishop. An old-fashioned, little-explored set-up that avoids the main-line theory.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and sets up on the long diagonal instead of defending e5 with a pawn. Quiet and solid but slow, so White can open the centre quickly and aim for a small edge; rarely played today.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Be7.strategy: A flexible developing move that prepares castling and expects to reach the main line of the Ruy Lopez by transposition. But Black has not yet put the question to the bishop, so White keeps more options open.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Be7.name: Ruy Lopez: Lucena Variation

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nd4.strategy: Counterattacks the bishop and the knight on f3 at once, a surprise that offers a trade. If White takes, Black recaptures with the pawn and gains space, but at the price of a slightly worse pawn structure. With careful play White is held to keep a small edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6.strategy: Defends e5 directly with a pawn, solid but passive and cramped. The pawn takes the king's bishop's best diagonal, and White can strike in the centre at once and force Black to give up the e5 pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f5.strategy: Strikes at the e4 pawn from the flank and sacrifices material for a kingside attack, ignoring the bishop. Sharp and a good practical weapon, but positionally risky: it loosens Black's own kingside and against a prepared opponent Black can end up in trouble.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop on the active diagonal toward f2 without worrying about the pressure on c6. But White can drive it back with pawn moves that also build the centre, so Black loses time; rarely played.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Bb4.strategy: Puts the bishop on an active diagonal but does nothing about the pressure on c6 and e5. White kicks it at once with a pawn move that also builds the centre, so Black loses time for little in return.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a5.strategy: A queenside pawn move that does nothing about the pressure on c6 and e5. Its only point is a trap: if White drifts, the bishop can be shut in on the queenside. Against sensible play Black has simply lost time.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a5.name: Ruy Lopez: Bulgarian Variation

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn but takes the natural f6 square from the king's knight and weakens the kingside, so Black's development becomes awkward and White is left with the easier game.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 f6.name: Ruy Lopez: Nürnberg Variation

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 b6.strategy: Prepares to put the bishop on the long diagonal but ignores the pressure on c6 and e5, and loosens the queenside. The gambit idea is dubious and White gets a comfortable game.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 b6.name: Ruy Lopez: Rotary-Albany Gambit

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Qe7.strategy: Protects e5 at once, but the queen blocks the king's bishop and is tied to a passive defence. Not refuted, yet Black's development is awkward and White develops with ease.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Qe7.name: Ruy Lopez: Vinogradov Variation

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g5.strategy: A reckless pawn thrust that aims to chase the knight from f3 but develops nothing and does nothing for e5. It cripples the kingside, so White can strike in the centre while Black's king is exposed.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 g5.name: Ruy Lopez: Brentano Gambit

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Na5.strategy: Sidesteps the bishop but takes the only defender away from e5, so White can capture the pawn at once. The knight on the rim does little, and Black has spent a move on a bad square.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Na5.name: Ruy Lopez: Pollock Defence

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nb8.strategy: Retreats the knight to where it started: Black wastes two moves, gives up the defence of e5, which White can capture at once, and has asked nothing of the bishop. A curiosity rather than a defence.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nb8.name: Ruy Lopez: Retreat Variation

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d5.strategy: Counterattacks in the centre at once, offering White the choice between two central pawns. But Black is behind in development and the bishop still presses on c6: if White takes on d5 and the queen recaptures, Nc3 hits it with gain of time.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and hits e4 in one move, the more combative of the two main replies. The price is that the knight blocks the queen's control of g5, so Black must be ready for an attack on f7 and has to know the theory; in return Black gets active counterplay.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5.strategy: Mirrors White's bishop and keeps the queen's control of g5, so there is no sudden attack on f7. A slower, more positional choice than the sharp alternative, in which the fight is over the d4 square and which side builds the centre first.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7.strategy: A cautious reply that avoids the sharp lines and keeps the position solid, but does little to challenge White's centre. Black accepts a slightly cramped game: White has more space and freer development, and Black plays mostly for safety.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 h6.strategy: Takes g5 away from White's knight in advance, so that ...Nf6 can follow without allowing an attack on f7. The cost is a move spent on a pawn, which gives White time for a strike in the centre. A sound but slow precaution.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 h6.name: Italian Game: Anti-Fried Liver Defence

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 d6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn and keeps the position solid, an old-fashioned set-up. It restricts the king's bishop and leaves White the space and the choice of plan, but there is little to refute.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 d6.name: Italian Game: Paris Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 d6.background: 3...d6, also called the Semi-Italian Opening, was popular in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries but is rarely seen today.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nd4.strategy: Moves the same knight again and offers the e5 pawn as bait: after the greedy capture on e5, ...Qg5 attacks the knight and g2, and a further grab on f7 walks into a smothered mate. If White simply trades on d4, Black has wasted time and stands worse.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nd4.name: Italian Game: Blackburne-Kostić Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nd4.background: Wilhelm Steinitz made the first known mention of the line in 1895, in the addenda to his Modern Chess Instructor, and Borislav Kostić played it in the early twentieth century. Blackburne reputedly won a shilling a game with its trap, though no games of his with it are recorded.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 f5.strategy: A counter-gambit that weakens Black's own king: the c4 bishop already looks straight at g8, which makes castling short awkward, and the e8-h5 diagonal is open. White meets it by striking in the centre and keeps a clear edge.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 f5.name: Italian Game: Rousseau Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 f5.background: Named after the French master Eugène Rousseau; it is also called the Ponziani Countergambit, after Domenico Lorenzo Ponziani.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Be2 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and attacks the e4 pawn at once: White's quiet bishop move does not guard it, so White has to react. Black has a comfortable, natural position and can choose between solid and active set-ups.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5.strategy: Attacks e4 straight away and exploits what c3 cost White: after a trade on d5 the queen cannot be chased by a knight on c3. Black takes the initiative in the centre, and White needs a pin to keep the e5 pawn under pressure.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6.strategy: The safest reply: Black develops with an attack on the loose e4 pawn, so White has to commit the centre at once. Play can run from quiet and drawish, where White has a little more space, to very sharp.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 f5.strategy: Counterattacks at once with a pawn against e4, but the pawn move loosens Black's own king side. An aggressive surprise weapon that gives White the better game with correct play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nge7.strategy: Develops the knight to e7, ready for ...d5 without a knight on f6 for a later e5 to hit with tempo. But it does nothing about e4, and White's hold on the centre gives the better chances.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Nge7.name: Ponziani Opening: Réti Variation

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Be7.strategy: A passive developing move that ignores the loose e4 pawn and lets White build the pawn centre with no opposition. It was once thought to equalise, but it gives Black no counterplay against the centre.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Be7.name: Ponziani Opening: Romanishin Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 Be7.background: Oleg Romanishin tried 3...Be7 in the 1970s, and Batsford's highlighted it as equalising.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks the pawn on e4 at once, which White's third move left without a defender, so White has to spend a move on it. Black develops with a gain of time against an unusual set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d3 f5.strategy: A counterattack on e4 that opens the king's side too early. The e5 pawn depends on the knight for its defence, and after exf5 Black is simply a pawn down for a risky attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4.strategy: The normal capture. Black has no good way to hold the pawn on e5, so it is exchanged for White's d-pawn and the centre opens: White's pieces become active, Black's develop easily, and the game is level.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Nxd4.strategy: Trades knights, but after the exchanges White's queen lands on d4, where it cannot easily be driven away. Black has used time and a developed piece to take the pawn, and has handed White the better central control.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the second knight and keeps the position symmetrical and solid. Black takes no risks, but White decides the character of the game, which tends to be quiet and drawish, and Black has little scope to unbalance it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bb4.strategy: Develops the bishop and hits the knight, but it is early: the d2 pawn still stands behind the knight, so there is no pin, and White can jump to d5, attacking the bishop and gaining time.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the bishop to g7, aiming it down the long diagonal, but it is slow: White can open the centre before Black is ready, and Black has to catch up in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 f5.strategy: Gambits the f-pawn to hit e4, but it weakens Black's own king and White can simply take the pawn. Black has little to show for the sacrifice.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 f5.name: Three Knights Opening: Winawer Defence

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nxe5 Nxe5.strategy: Takes the knight, which wins a piece for a pawn: the e5 knight was attacked and White's last move gave it away for nothing. Black can simply take; there is no reason to decline.
